newsitem.title: UK: Commodity markets mostly edge up but coffee drops.
newsitem.headline: Commodity markets mostly edge up but coffee drops.

text.p: Gold, wheat and oil prices staged rallies on Monday in generally firmer world commodity markets, but a sell-off hit coffee.
The benchmark London January contract for Robusta coffee futures fell as low as $1,422 before steadying.
Coffee was hit by persistent selling by traders and producers that was triggered by what traders called bearish U.S. market data released late on Friday.
The data from the watchdog Commodity Futures Trading Commission showed a big increase in long positions held by speculators.
The threat of the specs offloading their long positions unnerved both London and New York markets.
There was also market talk that a sizeable volume of coffee is pending grading by New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange warehouses.
Traders said news emerging from a weekend meeting of the Association of Producing Countries (ACPC) in Costa Rica had no immediate impact.
"They didn't say anything, did they?" said one.
An ACPC statement made no mention of tighter export curbs to support prices although it did highlight the chairman's power to call extraordinary meetings if needed.
The flagship industrial metal, copper, which rebounded above $2,000 per tonne last Thursday was back up just above that threshold on Monday after a lurch downward late Friday.
Copper snapped up again on Monday on short-covering and speculative buying but technical resistance was seen at $2,040 per tonne.
Benchmark Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat was also firmer on short-covering at around $3.85 per bushel by the mid-session which was some 10 cents above values seen last week.

Gold also ended in London just firmer at $380.75 after $378.95 per ounce. Short covering was again largely responsible for the rise but volumes were thin with U.S. banks closed for the Veteran's Day holiday, dealers said.
A winter chill blew across much of Europe and the United States on Monday, raising a prospect of brisk demand for heating fuel and boosting world oil prices.
But the gains were swiftly sold in to amid signs that stocks of crude and crude products might be on the rise, albeit from low levels.
The benchmark December Brent Blend of crude oil reached $23.31 per barrel before easing to around $23, consolidating gains from a late Friday rally of 77 cents.
Freight rates again moved higher and the Baltic Freight Index (BFI) stood above 1,500 points for the first time since January 31.

The index is compiled by the Baltic Exchange in London based on rates for key routes. Stronger-than-expected demand for grains and minerals in Asia has caused a 50 percent rise in chartering rates since September.
The index rose 25 on Monday to 1,502.
